content: The Rotavirus Vaccine Program is an initiative aimed at reducing the rates of illness and death among children caused by diarrheal diseases, specifically those resulting from rotavirus infections. This program focuses on accelerating the availability of vaccines that are suitable for use in developing countries, where the burden of rotavirus-related disease is most severe. Each year, rotavirus is responsible for the deaths of over 600,000 children and the hospitalization of an additional two million. The majority of these deaths occur in developing nations, where access to adequate medical treatment is limited. However, it is important to note that nearly every child worldwide will experience at least one episode of rotavirus-induced diarrhea by the age of five. In response to this global health challenge, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the Rotavirus Vaccine Program in 2003 to address child morbidity and mortality by facilitating the introduction of rotavirus vaccines in resource-limited settings. In 1998, a rotavirus vaccine was licensed for use in the United States. Clinical trials conducted in the U.S., Finland, and Venezuela demonstrated that this vaccine was 80% to 100% effective in preventing severe diarrhea caused by rotavirus A. Furthermore, these studies did not identify any statistically significant serious adverse effects. However, the vaccine was withdrawn from the market in 1999 after it was discovered that it might increase the risk of intussusception, a form of bowel obstruction, in approximately one out of every 12,000 vaccinated infants. This incident sparked a heated debate regarding the balance of risks and benefits associated with rotavirus vaccination. By 2006, two new vaccines targeting rotavirus A infections were shown to be both safe and effective in children. One of these vaccines, Rotarix, is manufactured by GlaxoSmithKline. It is an oral vaccine that contains a live, attenuated human rotavirus strain with G1P specificity. The second vaccine, RotaTeq, is produced by Merck. It is a live, oral pentavalent vaccine that contains five rotavirus strains created through reassortment. These reassortant strains are derived from both human and bovine rotavirus parent strains. Four of the reassortant viruses express one of the outer capsid proteins, VP7, corresponding to human rotavirus serotypes G1, G2, G3, or G4, while the attachment protein VP4 (type P7) is derived from the bovine rotavirus parent strain. The fifth reassortant virus expresses the VP4 attachment protein (type P1A) from the human rotavirus parent strain and the VP7 outer capsid protein (serotype G6) from the bovine rotavirus parent strain. In February 2006, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved RotaTeq for use in the United States. Merck is collaborating with various partners, including the Rotavirus Vaccine Program, PATH (Program for Appropriate Technology in Health), and other governmental and non-governmental organizations, to develop and implement strategies for ensuring access to this vaccine in developing countries.
